Grids#

dual_mesh

Return the DFT sample frequencies of a 2-D grid, both components.

shell_means

Return the mean of a spectrum over shells of constant |q|.

ShellMeans

Shell frequencies and shell means of a spectrum.
scatterem.utils.spectral_mesh.dual_mesh(n_yx: Any, pitch: Any, *, staggered: bool, dtype: dtype | None = None, device: device | str | None = None) → Tensor#

Return the DFT sample frequencies of a 2-D grid, both components.

The frequencies of a sampled field form the dual (reciprocal) lattice of its sampling lattice. Each value is computed in exact rational arithmetic and then rounded once to the output dtype.

Parameters:

  • n_yx (sequence of int) – The number of grid points (Ny, Nx). Each count is a positive integer.

  • pitch (float or sequence of float) – The real-space pitch (d_y, d_x) [length]. One number applies to both axes. There is no default: give 1.0 for frequencies in cycles per sample.

  • staggered (bool) – If True, add half of the frequency step to each axis: 1 / (2 Ny d_y) and 1 / (2 Nx d_x). Use it for samples that sit midway between the grid points. Give False for the standard DFT grid. There is no default.

  • dtype (torch.dtype, optional) – torch.float32 or torch.float64. The default is torch.get_default_dtype().

  • device (torch.device or str, optional) – The device of the result. The default is the CPU.

Returns:

Shape (2, Ny, Nx) [1/length], in FFT order. Entry [0, i, j] is the y frequency of row i and entry [1, i, j] is the x frequency of column j. Entry 0 holds the y frequencies and entry 1 the x frequencies. Use torch.fft.fftshift(out, dim=(-2, -1)) to centre it.

Return type:

torch.Tensor

Raises:

  • TypeError – If a count is not an integer, a pitch is not a real number, or the dtype is not float32 or float64.

  • ValueError – If a count is smaller than 1, the number of pitches is not 2, or a pitch is not finite and positive.

scatterem.utils.spectral_mesh.shell_means(spectrum_samples: Any, pitch: Any) → ShellMeans#

Return the mean of a spectrum over shells of constant |q|.

Each sample has the frequency |q| = sqrt(q_0^2 + q_1^2 + ...) from the DFT frequencies of its axes (see dual_mesh). The shells are equally spaced in |q| with the spacing D = max_a 1 / (N_a d_a), the coarsest frequency step. Shell k is at q_k = k D.

A sample at |q| = x D with k0 = floor(x) and t = x - k0 gives the weight (1 - t) J to shell k0 and t J to shell k0 + 1 (linear interpolation). The factor J = (D / |q|)^(n - 1) for n axes cancels the growth of the number of samples with |q|, so the effective weight in |q| is a symmetric tent about q_k. The bias for a smooth f(|q|) is then about f''(q_k) D^2 / 12. The sample at |q| = 0 gives the weight 1 to shell 0. The shell mean is sum w v / sum w, so it is linear in the values and a constant array gives that constant.

Outer limit: q_lim is the smallest of the largest positive axis frequencies, min_a floor((N_a - 1) / 2) / (N_a d_a). The output holds the shells k with (k + 1) D <= q_lim: every shell in the output has all of its support inside the grid. The largest shell frequency is thus in [q_lim - 2 D, q_lim - D].

Parameters:

  • spectrum_samples (numpy.ndarray or torch.Tensor) – Real or integer array with two or more axes, in FFT order on every axis (zero frequency at the first element), for example abs(torch.fft.fftn(x)) ** 2. A tensor can be on any device.

  • pitch (float or sequence of float) – The real-space pitch of each axis [length], or one value for all axes. There is no default: give 1.0 for frequencies in cycles per sample.

Returns:

(shell_wavenumber, shell_average): two new NumPy float64 arrays of equal length. shell_wavenumber is in [1/length].

Return type:

ShellMeans

Raises:

  • TypeError – If spectrum_samples is complex, bool or not an array, or a pitch is not a real number.

  • ValueError – If spectrum_samples has fewer than two axes, an axis has fewer than 3 points, spectrum_samples holds NaN or infinite values, the number of pitches is wrong, or a pitch is not finite and positive.

class scatterem.utils.spectral_mesh.ShellMeans(shell_wavenumber: np.ndarray, shell_average: np.ndarray)#

Shell frequencies and shell means of a spectrum.

Parameters:

  • shell_wavenumber (numpy.ndarray) – Shape (K,), float64. The frequency of each shell [1/length], equally spaced and increasing, starting at 0.

  • shell_average (numpy.ndarray) – Shape (K,), float64. The weighted mean of the samples of each shell, in the unit of the input values.

Visualisation#

show_2d

Show 2D data as one panel or as a grid of panels.

show_2d_array

Draw panels into a grid of axes and return the figure and the axes.
scatterem.vis.visualization.show_2d(array, *, sampling=None, scalebar='auto', figax=None, axsize=(4, 4), tight_layout=True, combine_images=False, clip_percentile: tuple[float, float] | None = None, max_display_pixels: int | None = None, style: str | None = None, **kwargs)#

Show 2D data as one panel or as a grid of panels.

The input can be a numpy array, a torch tensor, or a list (or a list of lists) of them. A tensor goes to the CPU and becomes a numpy array. A 3D array is a stack: each slice gets a panel. The scale bar uses sampling; without it, the .sampling_meta of the input if it has one; else the bar reads 1 a.u..

Parameters:

  • array (numpy.ndarray or torch.Tensor or sequence) – The data. A list gives one row of panels; a list of lists gives rows.

  • sampling (Sampling or dict, optional) – Pixel size and units (a Sampling or a dict of its fields). Default is None: use array.sampling_meta if it exists.

  • scalebar ("auto", bool, dict, or ScalebarConfig, optional) – "auto" draws a calibrated bar when the sampling allows it. False or None still draw a bar, the “1 a.u.” bar. Default is “auto”.

  • figax (tuple, optional) – (fig, axes) to draw into; axes must match the panel grid. Default is None, which makes a new figure.

  • axsize (tuple of int, optional) – Width and height in inches of one panel of a new figure. Default is (4, 4).

  • tight_layout (bool, optional) – Call fig.tight_layout() at the end. Default is True.

  • combine_images (bool, optional) – Blend one row of arrays into a single image, one hue per array. Default is False.

  • clip_percentile (tuple of float, optional) – (low, high) percentiles (0-100) used to set each array’s display vmin/vmax. A centred role keeps limits symmetric about its centre. A cyclic role ignores it and warns. Default is None.

  • max_display_pixels (int or None, optional) – The most pixels shown along either image axis. Larger images are block-averaged by one integer factor (no aliasing); every scale-bar sampling follows, and ticks and overlays use display pixels. None (the default) shows every pixel.

  • style ({"screen", "paper"}, optional) – Draw with the text and line sizes of show(style=...) (figure_params()). The axes of figax get the tick, axis-label and spine sizes too. Save the figure inside use_style(style=...): the dpi, the PDF font type and the font are read when the figure is saved or drawn.

  • **kwargs – Forwarded to show_2d_array(). Common keys: role (kind of data, e.g. “intensity” (default), “signed”, “angle”; sets colour map and limits), background (“light” or “dark”), cmap (overrides the role’s map) and cbar (colour bar; default True).

Returns:

  • fig (matplotlib.figure.Figure) – The figure that holds the panels.

  • axs (matplotlib.axes.Axes or numpy.ndarray of matplotlib.axes.Axes) – One Axes for one panel. A 1D array for a single row or column of panels, and a 2D array for a grid.

scatterem.vis.visualization.show_2d_array(arrays: NDArray | Sequence[NDArray] | Sequence[Sequence[NDArray]], *, figax: tuple[Any, Any] | None = None, axsize: tuple[int, int] = (4, 4), tight_layout: bool = True, combine_images: bool = False, scalebar: Any = 'auto', sampling: Sampling | None = None, scalebar_panel: Any = 'first', clip_percentile: tuple[float, float] | None = None, **kwargs: Any) → tuple[Any, Any]#

Draw panels into a grid of axes and return the figure and the axes.

show_2d() converts and bounds its input, then calls this function. Each panel is drawn by _show_2d. With combine_images, the one row of panels is blended into one image by _show_2d_combined instead.

Parameters:

  • arrays (ndarray or sequence of ndarray or sequence of sequences of ndarray) – One 2D array, a 3D stack (one panel per slice), a list (one row), or a list of lists (one row per inner list; rows can be short).

  • figax (tuple, optional) – (fig, axes) to draw into. axes is one Axes or a numpy array of them, with the shape of the panel grid (a 1D array counts as one row). Default is None, which makes a new figure.

  • axsize (tuple, default=(4, 4)) – Width and height in inches of one panel of a new figure.

  • tight_layout (bool, default=True) – Call fig.tight_layout() after drawing.

  • combine_images (bool, default=False) – Blend a single row of arrays into one image, one hue per array. Only norm, cmap, chroma_boost, cbar and figsize are accepted in kwargs then.

  • scalebar ("auto", bool, dict, or ScalebarConfig, default="auto") – The scale bar of the panels that scalebar_panel selects.

  • sampling (Sampling, optional) – Pixel size and units for the scale bar and the colour-bar unit.

  • scalebar_panel ("first", "all", or int, default="first") – Panels with a bar: the first, all, or the one at this flat index (row by row).

  • clip_percentile (tuple of (float, float), optional) – (low, high) percentiles (0-100). Each panel then gets the limits of these percentiles of its own finite values (the modulus, for complex data), as a manual interval. It replaces norm.

  • **kwargs (dict) – Passed to every panel, for example norm, cmap, role or cbar. title is special: one string for all panels, a flat list (row by row), or a list of lists.

Returns:

  • fig (Figure) – The figure that holds the panels.

  • axs (Axes or ndarray of Axes) – One Axes for a 1 x 1 grid, a 1D array for one row or one column, and a 2D array otherwise.

Raises:

  • ValueError – If the axes of figax do not have the grid shape, or if combine_images gets several rows or a per-panel keyword.

  • NotImplementedError – If combine_images is used with cbar=True.

Parameters:

Returns:

"gpaw" or "hydrogenic".

scatterem.simulation.eels.physics.radial.hydrogenic_bound_wavefunction(Z: int, n: int, l: int, n_points: int | None = None, rmax: float = 40.0) → AtomicRadialWavefunction#

Normalised hydrogenic bound state on a uniform grid.

With rho = 2 Z r / n, R_nl = N rho^l exp(-rho/2) L^(2l+1)_(n-l-1)(rho) and N = sqrt((2Z/n)^3 (n-l-1)! / (2n (n+l)!)), where L is the generalised Laguerre polynomial with L^(a)_k(0) = binom(k+a, k). The energy is -Z^2/(2 n^2) Hartree.

The default grid has at least 4000 points and at least 10 points per orbital length n / Z Bohr, so a heavy K shell is sampled as finely as a light one.

Parameters:

  • Z (int) – Effective nuclear charge.

  • n (int) – Principal quantum number.

  • l (int) – Orbital angular-momentum quantum number, must satisfy 0 <= l < n.

  • n_points (int, optional) – Number of samples on the radial grid linspace(0, rmax, n_points). None (default) chooses it from Z / n as described above.

  • rmax (float, optional) – Outer edge of the radial grid, in Bohr.

Returns:

The normalised hydrogenic bound state u(r) = r * R_nl(r).

Return type:

AtomicRadialWavefunction

Raises:

ValueError – If l is not in 0 <= l < n.

scatterem.simulation.eels.physics.radial.free_continuum_wavefunction(l: int, epsilon: float, n_points: int = 8000, rmax: float = 60.0) → AtomicRadialWavefunction#

Free continuum state, normalised per Rydberg.

u(r) = (pi k)^(-1/2) k r j_l(k r), with k = sqrt(epsilon / Ry) in 1/Bohr. Far out u -> (pi k)^(-1/2) sin(k r - l pi/2), so int u_E u_E' dr = delta(E - E') with E in Ry (Manson 1972).

Parameters:

  • l (int) – Orbital angular-momentum quantum number of the continuum state.

  • epsilon (float) – Energy above the ionization threshold, in eV. Must be > 0.

  • n_points (int, optional) – Number of samples on the radial grid linspace(0, rmax, n_points).

  • rmax (float, optional) – Outer edge of the radial grid, in Bohr.

Returns:

The free spherical-Bessel continuum state u_l(r), units Bohr^(-1/2) Ry^(-1/2).

Return type:

AtomicRadialWavefunction

Raises:

ValueError – If epsilon <= 0.

Phase

One crystalline phase: a general cell and its P1 sites (immutable).
class scatterem.crystal.phase.Phase(cell, fractional, element_z, *, site_fraction=None, msd=None, adp=None, name: str = '', point_group: str | None = None)#

One crystalline phase: a general cell and its P1 sites (immutable).

Parameters:

  • cell (array_like) – Shape (3, 3), any real dtype, Angstrom. The cell edge vectors as rows; any orientation, orthogonal or oblique, right- or left-handed.

  • fractional (array_like) – Shape (N, 3), any real dtype. Site positions as fractions of the cell edges (component i along row i of cell). N may be 0. Kept as given (no wrap).

  • element_z (array_like) – Shape (N,), integers 1 to 118. Atomic number of each site row.

  • site_fraction (None, float or array_like, optional) – (N,) or scalar, in [0, 1]. Occupancy of each row; None means full. A mixed site has one row per species, all at the same position. Checked as in AtomSet.

  • msd (None, float or array_like, optional) – (N,) or scalar, Angstrom^2, >= 0. Isotropic mean-square displacement <u^2> along one direction. None gives DEFAULT_U2.

  • adp (None or array_like, optional) – Shape (N, 3, 3), Angstrom^2. Symmetric anisotropic displacement tensors U, Cartesian in the frame of the cell rows. None (default) means isotropic sites (msd only). A structure factor uses a tensor as exp(-2 pi^2 g^T U g).

  • name (str, optional) – Free-form label.

  • point_group (str or None, optional) – Hermann-Mauguin point-group symbol, if known. No code reads it yet.

Raises:

ValueError – For a bad argument. The message starts with the argument name.

Notes

The arrays are read-only and every property returns the stored array.

Fourier helpers#

phase_ramp

Build the Fourier phase ramp that shifts a grid of shape by shift.

fourier_shift

Shift x by shift pixels along its last axes (Fourier shift theorem).

fourier_rescale

Resample x to a new pixel size by cropping or zero-padding its spectrum.

dft_center

Return the index of the zero frequency in a spectrum of real-space shape.

fftshift_last2

Return torch.fft.fftshift(x, dim=(-2, -1)), bit-identical, ONE buffer.

fftshift_rfft

Apply fftshift to every spatial axis of an rfft spectrum but the last.

ifftshift_rfft

Undo fftshift_rfft().

rfft_shape

Return the shape of torch.fft.rfftn over every axis of shape.
scatterem.physics.fourier.phase_ramp(shape: Sequence[int], shift: Sequence[float] | Tensor, *, rfft: bool = False, dtype: dtype = torch.complex64, ramp_dtype: dtype = torch.float64, device: str | device | None = None) → Tensor#

Build the Fourier phase ramp that shifts a grid of shape by shift.

The ramp is exp(-2j * pi * (k_0 * s_0 + k_1 * s_1 + ...)), summed in axis order, with k_i the fftfreq (cycles per pixel) of axis i. Multiplying a spectrum by it and transforming back moves the content by +shift pixels.

For real x, irfftn(rfftn(x) * phase_ramp(x.shape, s, rfft=True), x.shape) equals fourier_shift(x, s) (up to rounding) only when no axis but the last carries Nyquist content: exactly so on odd grids, on grids even only in the last axis, and for data with nothing in the Nyquist planes of the other axes. On white noise with an even non-last axis the two differ, because fourier_shift() keeps the real part of a full-spectrum shift there.

Parameters:

  • shape (sequence of int) – Real-space grid shape (n_0, ..., n_{D-1}).

  • shift (sequence of float or Tensor) – Shift in pixels: a host sequence of length D (each entry a float or a 0-d tensor, read with float()), or a tensor (..., D) whose leading axes become leading axes of the ramp. A sequence with an entry that requires grad is stacked and takes the tensor path, so gradients flow.

  • rfft (bool, optional) – Build the half spectrum of torch.fft.rfftn: the last axis has n_{D-1} // 2 + 1 non-negative frequencies. Default False.

  • dtype (torch.dtype, optional) – Complex dtype of the returned ramp. Default torch.complex64.

  • ramp_dtype (torch.dtype, optional) – Real dtype the phase is computed in before the cast. Default torch.float64.

  • device (str or torch.device, optional) – Device of the ramp. Default: the shift’s device for a tensor shift (or a stacked sequence), otherwise the CPU.

Returns:

(..., *shape) ramp (last axis n_{D-1} // 2 + 1 when rfft).

Return type:

Tensor

Raises:

ValueError – If shift does not address exactly len(shape) axes.

scatterem.physics.fourier.fourier_shift(x: Tensor, shift: Sequence[float] | Tensor, *, ndim: int | None = None, ramp_dtype: dtype = torch.float64) → Tensor#

Shift x by shift pixels along its last axes (Fourier shift theorem).

Periodic; equals torch.roll for whole-pixel shifts up to FFT rounding. For real input, a fractional shift on an even grid loses part of the Nyquist frequency component (the ramp is not Hermitian there, and the real part is returned), so it is not exactly power preserving. A host shift is read with float() (a device sync for 0-d CUDA tensors), unless an entry requires grad: then the entries are stacked and take the tensor path. A tensor shift stays on the device and carries gradients. With a batched tensor shift, CPU results equal a per-slice loop only up to floating-point rounding. The rfft route irfftn(rfftn(x) * phase_ramp(..., rfft=True)) agrees with this function for real x only under the Nyquist condition phase_ramp() states.

Parameters:

  • x (Tensor) – Real or complex (..., n_0, ..., n_{D-1}); the last D axes move.

  • shift (sequence of float or Tensor) – Shift in pixels, array order: a host sequence of length D, or a tensor (..., D) whose leading axes broadcast against the leading axes of x.

  • ndim (int, optional) – Number of shifted axes D. Default: inferred from shift; when given it must agree with it.

  • ramp_dtype (torch.dtype, optional) – Real dtype of the phase ramp before it is cast to the spectrum’s complex dtype. Default torch.float64.

Returns:

The shifted array. Complex input keeps its dtype; real floating input returns the real part in its dtype; integer input returns the real part in torch’s default floating dtype.

Return type:

Tensor

Raises:

ValueError – If shift and ndim disagree, D exceeds x.ndim, or the leading shapes of a tensor shift and x do not broadcast.

scatterem.physics.fourier.fourier_rescale(x: Tensor, sampling_in: Sequence[float], sampling_out: Sequence[float], *, ndim: int | None = None, taper: float | None = None) → tuple[Tensor, tuple[float, ...]]#

Resample x to a new pixel size by cropping or zero-padding its spectrum.

This is the anti-aliased down-sampling: every frequency above the new Nyquist frequency is removed, not folded back. A box average (F.interpolate(mode="area")) folds a crystal lattice above the new Nyquist frequency onto the coarse grid. taper adds a raised-cosine roll-off below the band edge, which removes the ringing of a hard cut.

Axis i gets round(n_i * sampling_in[i] / sampling_out[i]) samples (half rounds up). The band-limited interpolant is preserved: up-sampling by an integer factor reproduces the input at the original sample positions, and the mean value is unchanged. Sample 0 stays at the origin (corner convention).

Parameters:

  • x (Tensor) – Real or complex (..., n_0, ..., n_{D-1}); the last D axes are resampled.

  • sampling_in (sequence of float) – Pixel size of x per resampled axis.

  • sampling_out (sequence of float) – Requested pixel size per resampled axis.

  • ndim (int, optional) – Number of resampled axes D. Default len(sampling_in).

  • taper (float or None, optional) – Width of a raised-cosine roll-off, as a fraction of the band edge (the lower of the two Nyquist frequencies, per axis, on an elliptical radius). The weight is 1 below 1 - taper and 0 at the edge; the DC weight is 1, so the mean stays. None (the default) is a hard cut. The roll-off also applies when no axis changes size.

Returns:

  • rescaled (Tensor) – The resampled array; real input gives real output in its dtype, and integer input a floating array (never truncated back to integers). When no axis changes size, x itself is returned, not a copy.

  • sampling (tuple of float) – The pixel size actually achieved, n_i * sampling_in[i] / n_out_i; exactly sampling_in[i] on an axis whose size did not change.

Raises:

ValueError – If the sampling lengths disagree with ndim, ndim exceeds x.ndim, a sampling is not finite and positive, an axis would get fewer than one sample, or taper is not in (0, 1].

scatterem.physics.fourier.dft_center(shape: Sequence[int], *, rfft: bool, fftshifted: bool) → tuple[int, ...]#

scatterem.physics.fourier.ifftshift_rfft(x: Tensor, ndim: int) → Tensor#

  • ndim (int) – Number of spatial axes D.

Returns:

x with its zero frequency back at index 0 on axes 0 .. D-2.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.physics.fourier.rfft_shape(shape: Sequence[int]) → tuple[int, ...]#

Return the shape of torch.fft.rfftn over every axis of shape.

Parameters:

shape (sequence of int) – Real-space shape.

Returns:

shape with its last entry replaced by shape[-1] // 2 + 1.

Return type:

tuple of int

Axis-angle rotations#

to_matrix

Return the matrices of right-handed turns by angle about axis.
scatterem.rotation.axis_angle.to_matrix(axis: Tensor, angle: Tensor) → Tensor#

Return the matrices of right-handed turns by angle about axis.

Parameters:

  • axis (Tensor) – Rotation axes with shape (..., 3). They need not be unit vectors, but must not be zero.

  • angle (Tensor) – Rotation angles in radians with shape (...), broadcastable with the batch shape of axis.

Returns:

Rotation matrices with shape (..., 3, 3). R @ v turns a column vector v counter-clockwise about axis when seen from its tip.

Return type:

Tensor

Notes

Three dtype rules apply, as in scatterem.rotation.quaternion.from_axis_angle():

  • The output dtype is the type promotion of axis and angle.

  • sin and cos of the half angle run in the dtype of angle (the default float dtype for an integer angle). A float32 angle with a float64 axis gives a float64 matrix with float32 accuracy.

  • An integer axis is refused: torch.linalg.vector_norm raises RuntimeError.

The quaternion route agrees with Rodrigues’ formula cos(angle) I + sin(angle) K + (1 - cos(angle)) u u^T to a few ulp, but not bit for bit.

Examples

>>> import math, torch
>>> from scatterem.rotation.axis_angle import to_matrix
>>> R = to_matrix(torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]), torch.tensor(math.pi / 2))
>>> torch.allclose(R @ torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]),
...                torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), atol=1e-6)
True

Quaternions#

from_axis_angle

Build the quaternions of right-handed turns about axes.

from_matrix

Convert rotation matrices to quaternions.

from_rotation_vector

Build the unit quaternions of rotation vectors.

multiply

Compute the Hamilton product q1 ⊗ q2.

to_matrix

Convert quaternions to rotation matrices.
scatterem.rotation.quaternion.from_axis_angle(axis: Tensor, angle: Tensor) → Tensor#

Build the quaternions of right-handed turns about axes.

The quaternion is (cos(angle / 2), sin(angle / 2) * axis / |axis|). The function multiplies by the sine first and divides by the axis norm after, so a single turn about a coordinate axis has exact bits.

Parameters:

  • axis (torch.Tensor) – Rotation axes with shape (..., 3). They need not be unit vectors, but must not be zero.

  • angle (torch.Tensor) – Rotation angles in radians with shape (...), broadcastable with the batch shape of axis.

Returns:

Unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4). w is negative for |angle| > pi; the function does not fold the sign.

Return type:

torch.Tensor

Notes

Three dtype rules apply:

  • The output dtype is the type promotion of axis and angle.

  • sin and cos of the half angle run in the dtype of angle (the default float dtype for an integer angle). A float32 angle with a float64 axis gives a float64 result with float32 accuracy.

  • An integer axis is refused: torch.linalg.vector_norm raises RuntimeError.

scatterem.rotation.quaternion.from_matrix(m: Tensor) → Tensor#

Convert rotation matrices to quaternions.

Parameters:

m (torch.Tensor) – Rotation matrices with shape (..., 3, 3).

Returns:

Unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4), with w >= 0.

Return type:

torch.Tensor

scatterem.rotation.quaternion.from_rotation_vector(w: Tensor) → Tensor#

Build the unit quaternions of rotation vectors.

The rotation is exp([w]_x): the angle is |w| in radians and the axis is w. The quaternion is (cos(|w| / 2), sin(|w| / 2) w / |w|). The function writes sin(|w| / 2) / |w| as sinc(|w| / 2 pi) / 2, so it is smooth at w = 0 and has a finite gradient there. That is where every gradient refinement of an orientation starts. Unlike from_axis_angle(), it accepts the zero vector, which gives the identity (1, 0, 0, 0).

Parameters:

w (torch.Tensor) – Rotation vectors with shape (..., 3), in radians.

Returns:

Unit quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4), in the dtype of w. to_matrix of the result is the rotation matrix exp([w]_x).

Return type:

torch.Tensor

scatterem.rotation.quaternion.multiply(q1: Tensor, q2: Tensor) → Tensor#

Compute the Hamilton product q1 ⊗ q2.

The result applies rotation q2 followed by q1, matching the composition R1 @ R2 of the corresponding rotation matrices.

Parameters:

  • q1 (torch.Tensor) – Quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4).

  • q2 (torch.Tensor) – Quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4), broadcastable with q1.

Returns:

Hamilton product quaternions with shape (..., 4).

Return type:

torch.Tensor

scatterem.rotation.quaternion.to_matrix(q: Tensor) → Tensor#

Convert quaternions to rotation matrices.

Parameters:

q (torch.Tensor) – Quaternions (w, x, y, z) with shape (..., 4). Not required to be unit norm; normalized internally.

Returns:

Rotation matrices with shape (..., 3, 3).

Return type:

torch.Tensor

scatterem.vis.register_colormaps() → None#

Register every Crameri map with matplotlib under its bare name.

cmcrameri registers "cmc.batlow". This adds "batlow" and "batlow_r" too. Names matplotlib already has (berlin, managua, vanimo: the same tables) are left alone. Nothing else in matplotlib changes. The function runs once per process.

class scatterem.vis.ColourChoice(cmap: Colormap, cls: str, kind: str, trail: tuple[tuple[str, object], ...], centre: float | None = None, period: float | None = None)#

  • trail (tuple of (str, object)) – Each Fig. 6 question and its answer, in order.

  • centre (float, optional) – Central value of diverging and multi-sequential data.

  • period (float, optional) – Period of cyclic data.

class scatterem.vis.DataTraits(ordered: bool = True, centre: float | None = None, ordered_about_centre: bool = True, period: float | None = None, small_variations: bool = True, levels: int | None = None, intuitive: str | None = None)#

The answers to the questions of Fig. 6 of Crameri et al. (2020).

Parameters:

  • ordered (bool, default=True) – Has the data an order? False gives a categorical map.

  • centre (float, optional) – The central value of the data, if it has one (for example 0).

  • ordered_about_centre (bool, default=True) – With a centre: True gives a diverging map, False a multi-sequential one.

  • period (float, optional) – The period of periodic data (for example 2 * pi); gives a cyclic map. show_2d wraps the values into [-period/2, period/2), so data on any interval of one period shows correctly.

  • small_variations (bool, default=True) – Must small variations show? True gives a continuous map, False discrete.

  • levels (int, optional) – Number of colours of a discrete map. Default 10.

  • intuitive (str, optional) – A map with colours that suit the parameter, if there is one. A map outside the scientific allow-list warns.

class scatterem.vis.NormalizationConfig(interval_type: str = 'quantile', stretch_type: str = 'linear', lower_quantile: float = 0.02, upper_quantile: float = 0.98, vmin: float | None = None, vmax: float | None = None, vcenter: float = 0.0, half_range: float | None = None, power: float = 1.0, logarithmic_index: float = 1000.0, asinh_linear_range: float = 0.1)#

Settings for CustomNormalization.

Parameters:

  • interval_type ({"quantile", "manual", "centered"}) – How (vmin, vmax) are chosen. "quantile" uses the lower_quantile/upper_quantile of the finite data, "manual" uses vmin/vmax (falling back to the finite data range for either one left as None), "centered" uses vcenter +/- half_range (half_range defaults to the largest finite deviation from vcenter).

  • stretch_type ({"linear", "power", "logarithmic", "asinh"}) – Which stretch to apply; see _stretch_pair() for the formulas.

  • lower_quantile (float) – Quantiles in [0, 1] with lower < upper, used by "quantile".

  • upper_quantile (float) – Quantiles in [0, 1] with lower < upper, used by "quantile".

  • vmin (float, optional) – Explicit limits, used by "manual".

  • vmax (float, optional) – Explicit limits, used by "manual".

  • vcenter (float, optional) – Center and half-width, used by "centered".

  • half_range (float, optional) – Center and half-width, used by "centered".

  • power (float) – Exponent p > 0 of the "power" stretch.

  • logarithmic_index (float) – Curvature a > 0 of the "logarithmic" stretch.

  • asinh_linear_range (float) – Linear-range parameter a > 0 of the "asinh" stretch.

class scatterem.vis.CustomNormalization(config: NormalizationConfig | None = None, *, data: Any = None, clip: bool = False, **overrides: Any)#

Map data into [0, 1] for display: interval selection, then a stretch.

Parameters:

  • config (NormalizationConfig, optional) – Settings; defaults to NormalizationConfig().

  • data (array-like, optional) – Data used to resolve the limits immediately, so that vmin/vmax are populated before the first call (a colorbar needs them). Otherwise the limits are resolved on the first call, from the array passed there.

  • clip (bool) – Accepted for matplotlib.colors.Normalize compatibility. The result is confined to [0, 1] in any case, because the normalized value is clipped before the stretch is applied.

  • **overrides – Any NormalizationConfig field, passed directly instead of config.

Notes

The limits are resolved once and then frozen, whether by data= here or by the first call. One instance therefore describes one interval, which is what makes it safe to share across several images: they are all mapped through the same limits, and a colorbar drawn from those limits describes all of them. Pass a fresh instance per image to normalize each by its own limits.

scatterem.vis.draw_scale_bar(ax: Axes, n_pixels: float, pixel_size: float | None = None, unit: str | None = None, length: float | None = None, location: str | int = 'lower right', color: str = 'white', thickness: float = 0.014, margin: float = 0.035, label: bool = True, fontsize: float | None = None, outline: bool = True) → float#

Draw a scale bar on ax and return the length it represents.

Parameters:

  • ax (matplotlib.axes.Axes) – Axes holding the image. Its data limits are not read (the bar sits in axes fractions), but n_pixels must describe the displayed array.

  • n_pixels (float) – Width of the displayed array, in pixels.

  • pixel_size (float, optional) – Physical size of one pixel. None marks the image as uncalibrated: the bar is still drawn, one fifth of the field wide, labelled “1 a.u.”.

  • thickness (float, default=0.014) – Bar height, as a fraction of the axes height.

  • margin (float, default=0.035) – Gap between the bar and the axes edges, as a fraction of the axes (0.035 is 3.5 % in from the corner).

  • fontsize (float, optional) – Label size in points. None scales it to the bar thickness.

  • outline (bool, default=True) – Stroke the bar and label in black, so a white bar stays legible over a light region of the image.

float

Where and how the plot functions draw a scale bar.

  • length (float, optional) – Bar length in units. None picks the longest 1-2-5 length that fits in a third of the image width.

  • width_px (float, default=1) – Thickness of the scale bar, in data pixels.

  • pad_px (float, default=0.5) – Padding between the bar and the axes corner, in multiples of the label font size (not pixels, despite the name – this is the AnchoredSizeBar convention). Values above a few push the bar out of the corner and into the image.

  • loc (str or int, default="lower right") – Corner that holds the bar, as a matplotlib legend location: a name such as "upper left" or its integer code.

Colour an image, using phase as hue when it is given.

scatterem.vis.complex_color.phase_wheel(n: int = 256, *, lightness: float = 0.72, chroma: float = 0.13)#

(colors, angles) for a phase colorbar: one full turn of hue.

lightness is fixed so the bar reads as hue alone. The default sits near the middle of the range where the sRGB gamut is widest, so the wheel keeps its chroma all the way round instead of desaturating at some hues.

scatterem.vis.complex_color.tile_to_rgba(rows, *, norm=None, cmap: str = 'gray', chroma: float = 0.13) → NDArray#

Composite a grid of same-shaped images into one RGBA mosaic.

Replaces list_of_arrays_to_rgba. Each entry is coloured independently and the results are tiled, so a bright panel cannot darken its neighbours – the alternative, one normalisation across the whole grid, makes every panel but the brightest unreadable.

Parameters:

  • rows – sequence of rows, each a sequence of same-shaped 2D arrays.

  • norm –

    callable mapping amplitude to [0, 1], applied to each panel. If omitted, each panel is scaled by its own finite min and max.

    This argument is not optional in spirit: complex_to_rgba() requires [0, 1] and clips, so handing it raw data silently renders a 0..1000 image as 99.9% pure white. An earlier version of this function did exactly that.

  • cmap – colormap for real-valued panels.

  • chroma – Oklab chroma for the phase hue of complex panels.

Scale bars#

Sampling

Per-axis image calibration.

reconstruction_sampling

The real-space pixel of an image reconstructed from a scanned dataset.
class scatterem.data.sampling.Sampling(pixel_size: tuple[float, ...] | None = None, units: tuple[str, ...] | None = None, value_unit: str | None = None)#

Per-axis image calibration.

Replaces the removed UnitTensor: numeric data stays a plain tensor/ndarray; this sidecar is threaded explicitly so units cannot vanish through tensor ops.

Parameters:

  • pixel_size (float or tuple of float, optional) – Physical size of one pixel along each axis, in axis order (dy, dx) for a 2D image. None means uncalibrated.

  • units (str or tuple of str, optional) – Unit string per axis, e.g. ("Å", "Å") (real space) or ("1/Å", "1/Å") (reciprocal space).

  • value_unit (str, optional) – Unit of the stored values, used for the colorbar label.

Examples

The scale bar reads the last axis; mismatched axis counts raise:

>>> from scatterem.data import Sampling
>>> s = Sampling(pixel_size=(0.1, 0.2), units=("A", "A"), value_unit="e")
>>> s.is_calibrated, s.scalebar_sampling()
(True, (0.2, 'A'))
>>> Sampling(pixel_size=(1.0,), units=("A", "A"))
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: pixel_size has 1 axes but units has 2
scatterem.data.sampling.reconstruction_sampling(dataset: Any, image: Any = None, *, shape: Sequence[int] | None = None) → Sampling#

The real-space pixel of an image reconstructed from a scanned dataset.

A reconstruction is up-sampled relative to the scan, so its pixel is smaller than the scan step. It covers the same field of view as the scan, so:

pixel_size = scan_step * scan_px / image_px

per axis. The formula reads the upsample factor off the output shape, so the caller need not know which factor upsample="nyquist" picked.

Parameters:

  • dataset (object) – The dataset the reconstruction came from. Its shape[:2] is the scan shape and its sampling[:2] the scan step. Its units[:2] label the axes when present, else ("Å", "Å").

  • image (array-like, optional) – The reconstruction. Its last two dimensions give the output shape.

  • shape (sequence of int, optional) – The output shape (H, W), in place of image.

Returns:

The pixel size (dy, dx) and the units of the two real-space axes.

Return type:

Sampling

Raises:

ValueError – If neither image nor shape is given, or the shape is not 2-D.

Saving and loading#

Serializable

Give a declared-schema class save() and load.

load_serializable

Read a file written by Serializable.save(), as one of candidates.

read_schema

The class, version and field list of a file, without constructing anything.

SerializationError

A file cannot be written, or cannot be loaded faithfully.

SCHEMA_VERSION

Bumped when the on-disk layout changes in a way older readers cannot handle.
class scatterem.utils.store.Serializable#

Give a declared-schema class save() and load.

Subclasses set SERIAL_FIELDS to the attribute names to persist, and must be constructible from those names as keyword arguments – or override _from_fields() if construction needs more than that. A field holding another Serializable (or a list of them) names the class it holds in SERIAL_NESTED; a tuple there allows any one of several classes.

A subclass that declares neither SERIAL_FIELDS nor _from_fields itself adds behaviour but not state, and a file it wrote loads as its nearest ancestor that does – a download wrapper whose constructor fetches data cannot be rebuilt from fields. A subclass that shares its ancestor’s schema and is built the same way says so with a class keyword, class Sub(Base, load_as_self=True), and then loads as itself.

scatterem.utils.store.load_serializable(path: str | Path, candidates: Sequence[type], *, device: str | device = 'cpu')#

Read a file written by Serializable.save(), as one of candidates.

Parameters:

  • path (str or pathlib.Path) – The HDF5 file.

  • candidates (sequence of type) – The classes the caller allows, each a Serializable subclass. Their subclasses are allowed too; nothing else is.

  • device (str or torch.device, optional) – Device every tensor field is placed on. Default "cpu".

Returns:

The loaded object.

Return type:

Serializable

Raises:

SerializationError – If the file is missing, has another schema version, holds no allowed class, or its field list disagrees with the class’s.

scatterem.utils.store.read_schema(path: str | Path) → dict[str, Any]#

The class, version and field list of a file, without constructing anything.

Useful for telling why a load was refused.

Parameters:

path (str or pathlib.Path) – A file written by Serializable.save().

Returns:

schema_version (int, -1 if absent), class (the stored class name), module (its module, None for files that predate it) and fields (the recorded field list).

Return type:

dict

anisotropic_tv_subgradient

Exact (sub)gradient of the mean anisotropic TV loss.

Exact gradient of the mean isotropic TV loss of total_variation_3d().

mean_abs_forward_diff

Mean absolute forward difference of vol along dim.

scatterem.nn.regularizers.tv.anisotropic_tv_subgradient(volume: Tensor) → Tensor#

Exact (sub)gradient of the mean anisotropic TV loss.

The loss is sum_axes mean_n |v[n+1] - v[n]| over the forward differences of each axis: total_variation_3d() with isotropic=False on a [D, H, W] volume. Its derivative is the discrete divergence of sign(grad v) scaled by 1 / numel(diff) of that axis: sign of each forward difference is subtracted at the left voxel and added at the right voxel. Away from ties this equals autograd of the loss; at a kink (a zero difference) the subgradient 0 is chosen, as autograd’s abs does. Pure tensor math (no autograd graph, no backward), so it can be injected straight into object.grad – cheaper than building a TV loss term and backpropagating it.

Parameters:

volume (Tensor) – Real floating dense volume, any number of dimensions. An axis with fewer than two voxels has no differences and contributes nothing (where the mean loss would be NaN).

Returns:

Subgradient of the mean anisotropic TV, same shape, dtype and device as volume.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.nn.regularizers.tv.isotropic_tv_subgradient(volume: Tensor, eps: float = 1e-08) → Tensor#

Exact gradient of the mean isotropic TV loss of total_variation_3d().

The loss is mean_i sqrt(dz^2 + dy^2 + dx^2 + eps) over the common interior i in [0, D-1) x [0, H-1) x [0, W-1), with forward differences d.[i] = v[i + e.] - v[i]. It couples the three axes through the per-voxel gradient norm, so it smooths more uniformly than the axis-separable anisotropic version. With eps > 0 the loss is smooth, so this is its gradient everywhere, computed analytically without autograd.

Parameters:

  • volume (Tensor) – Real floating dense [D, H, W] volume. When an axis has fewer than two voxels the interior is empty and the result is all zeros (where the mean loss would be NaN).

  • eps (float, optional) – Smoothing term inside the gradient-norm square root, by default 1.0e-8, the default of total_variation_3d().

Returns:

Gradient of the mean isotropic TV, shape [D, H, W], on the dtype and device of volume.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.nn.regularizers.tv.mean_abs_forward_diff(vol: Tensor, dim: int) → Tensor#

Mean absolute forward difference of vol along dim.

Shared anisotropic-TV building block: mean(|vol[n+1] - vol[n]|) on axis dim. Used by total_variation_3d() (anisotropic).

Parameters:

  • vol (Tensor) – Real floating tensor of any shape.

  • dim (int) – Axis along which to take the forward difference. The axis length must be at least 2 or the mean is NaN.

Returns:

Scalar mean absolute difference on the dtype and device of vol.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.nn.regularizers.tv.total_variation_2d(image: Tensor, *, per_item: bool = False) → Tensor#

Mean anisotropic total variation over the last two axes of an image.

Forward differences: mean(|dH|) + mean(|dW|). When per_item is False the means cover the whole tensor; when True they reduce only the last two axes, returning one value per leading index. Matches the "tv" branch of the direct-ptychography image-sharpness metric.

Parameters:

  • image (Tensor) – Real floating image [..., H, W].

  • per_item (bool, optional) – Reduce only over H and W when True. Default False.

Returns:

Scalar mean TV, or a tensor of shape image.shape[:-2] when per_item is True.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.nn.regularizers.tv.total_variation_3d(vol: Tensor, isotropic: bool = True, eps: float = 1e-08) → Tensor#

Mean 3D total variation of a dense [D, H, W] volume (differentiable).

Isotropic: mean of sqrt(dz^2 + dy^2 + dx^2 + eps) over the common interior (edge-preserving, rotation-invariant). Anisotropic: sum of the mean absolute forward differences along each axis (cheaper, axis-aligned). Scale on this data: a converged 170^3 volume has TV ~1.6e-2 vs inner MSE ~2e-3, so tv_weight in 0.01-0.1 spans a gentle-to-strong prior.

Parameters:

  • vol (Tensor) – Real floating volume of shape (D, H, W). Differences are per voxel, without physical voxel-spacing normalization. Each axis must contain at least two voxels for a finite mean; an empty difference yields NaN.

  • isotropic (bool, optional) – Couple the three differences on the common interior when True; otherwise sum their separate mean absolute values. Default True.

  • eps (float, optional) – Squared-difference smoothing term for isotropic TV, default 1.0e-8. Ignored for anisotropic TV. Inputs and eps are not validated.

Returns:

Differentiable scalar mean TV on the input dtype and device.

Return type:

Tensor

scatterem.physics.kernels.lens_wavefront_wp.lens_wavefront_f32(lens: array(ndim=1, dtype=float32), fy: float32, fx: float32, lambda_a: float32) → float32#

Return the lens wavefront W [rad] at one frequency point, in float32.

Accuracy. For inputs that are exact in float32, the result W32 and the float64 value W64 of the same inputs satisfy:

|W32 - W64| <= 32 eps (2 pi / lambda) sum_j |c_j P_j| / (n_j + 1)
               + 4 eps |W64|,   eps = 2^-23,

with P_j the basis polynomial of slot j. Each term takes at most about 10 roundings, the sum of 12 terms adds 11 and the scaling adds 2.

Parameters:

  • lens (wp.array of wp.float32) – The 12 coefficients [Angstrom] in the order of LENS_LAYOUT.

  • fy (wp.float32) – Frequency coordinates k_y and k_x [1/Angstrom].

  • fx (wp.float32) – Frequency coordinates k_y and k_x [1/Angstrom].

  • lambda_a (wp.float32) – Wavelength [Angstrom], larger than zero.

Returns:

Wavefront [rad].

Return type:

wp.float32

scatterem.physics.kernels.lens_wavefront_wp.lens_wavefront_focus_f32(lens: array(ndim=1, dtype=float32), fy: float32, fx: float32, lambda_a: float32) → float32#

Return W [rad] for a lens vector whose sole non-zero slot is 0.

The function reads only lens[0] (the defocus slot C10). If the other 11 slots are +0.0 or -0.0 and all inputs are finite, it returns the same float32 bits as lens_wavefront_f32(). This needs the default Warp setting without fast-math; fast-math would void it.

Rule: the host picks lens_wavefront_focus_f32 or lens_wavefront_f32 before the launch (for example as a kernel template argument or by building one of two kernels). Do not choose between them inside a kernel with a run-time condition.

Parameters:

  • lens (wp.array of wp.float32) – The 12 coefficients [Angstrom] in the order of LENS_LAYOUT.

  • fy (wp.float32) – Frequency coordinates k_y and k_x [1/Angstrom].

  • fx (wp.float32) – Frequency coordinates k_y and k_x [1/Angstrom].

  • lambda_a (wp.float32) – Wavelength [Angstrom], larger than zero.

Returns:

Wavefront [rad].

Return type:

wp.float32

compute_ssnr_from_halfset_images

scatterem.reconstruction.darkfield.core.compute_ssnr_from_halfset_images(tcDF1, tcDF2, sampling, gaussian_sigma=0.0, verbosity=0)#

Estimate the radial spectral SNR from two independent half-set images.

Treats tcDF1/tcDF2 as two independent noise realizations of the same signal (N = (FA - FB) / 2 estimates the noise spectrum, S = (FA + FB) / 2 the signal-plus-noise spectrum), radially bins their power in Fourier space, and forms SSNR(q) = (S_power - N_power) / N_power.

Parameters:

  • tcDF1 (torch.Tensor) – First half-set real-space image, shape (H, W).

  • tcDF2 (torch.Tensor) – Second half-set real-space image, same shape as tcDF1.

  • sampling (tuple of float) – Real-space pixel sampling (dy, dx), used to build the Fourier frequency grid.

  • gaussian_sigma (float, optional) – If greater than 0, 1D-Gaussian-smooth the radial SSNR curve with this sigma, in radial bins.

  • verbosity (int, optional) – If greater than 1, plot the radial noise power, signal power and SSNR curves.

Returns:

The radial SSNR curve, the per-bin mean spatial frequency |q|, and the flattened per-pixel radial bin index (for scattering the radial curve back onto the 2D grid).

Return type:

tuple of (torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor)

scatterem.reconstruction.darkfield.drizzle#

drizzle_resample

Drizzle a stack of shifted frames onto a common up-sampled grid.
scatterem.reconstruction.darkfield.drizzle.drizzle_resample(images: Tensor, shifts: Tensor, upsample: int, *, pixfrac: float = 1.0, kde_sigma: float = 0.0, eps: float = 1e-12, return_parts: bool = False)#

Drizzle a stack of shifted frames onto a common up-sampled grid.

Runs under torch.no_grad: this is a resampling step, not part of an autograd path. Accumulation is forced to at least float32 – many index_add_ into a half-precision grid loses precision – and the normalized result is cast back to the input dtype.

Parameters:

  • images (Tensor) – Shape (N, H, W), real. The N dithered frames of the same scene, e.g. dark-field azimuthal-segment images. Non-negative input gives non-negative output.

  • shifts (Tensor) – Shape (N, 2), the per-frame (dy, dx) shift in output (HR) pixels. Frame n’s input pixel (i, j) is deposited at HR position (i * U + dy_n, j * U + dx_n): input pixel i maps to HR pixel i * U, matching Fourier zero-pad upsampling, plus the sub-pixel shift. Moved to the device and accumulation dtype of images.

  • upsample (int) – Integer output magnification U; the output is H * U by W * U.

  • pixfrac (float) – Drizzle drop size as a fraction of one input pixel, in (0, 1]. The deposited footprint is a box of side pixfrac * U HR pixels. A smaller value is sharper but needs denser coverage to avoid holes. Default 1.0.

  • kde_sigma (float) – When positive, Nadaraya-Watson smoothing: a Gaussian of this standard deviation in HR pixels is applied to numerator and denominator before dividing. Fills small holes and denoises, at the cost of resolution. Default 0.0.

  • eps (float) – Denominator floor, so uncovered output pixels read 0 rather than NaN. Default 1e-12.

  • return_parts (bool) – Also return the raw accumulation grids. Default False.

Returns:

The hit-normalised (H * U, W * U) image, in the dtype and on the device of images. With return_parts=True, the triple (image, accum, hits): accum is the flux grid, which conserves images.sum() for in-frame content, and hits is the summed coverage weight.

Return type:

Tensor or tuple of Tensor

Raises:

ValueError – If images is not 3-dimensional, if shifts is not (N, 2) matching it, if upsample is below 1, or if pixfrac is outside (0, 1].

scatterem.vis.normalization.INTERVAL_TYPES = ('quantile', 'manual', 'centered')#

Draw a colorbar for norm/cmap into an existing axes.

Parameters:

  • fig (matplotlib.figure.Figure) – The figure that gets the bar.

  • cax (matplotlib.axes.Axes) – The empty axes that the bar fills, for example from make_axes_locatable(ax).append_axes.

  • norm (matplotlib.colors.Normalize) – Value mapping of the image. Its vmin and vmax must be set; they bound the ticks.

  • cmap (matplotlib.colors.Colormap) – The colour map of the image.

  • eps (float, optional) – Tolerance when discarding ticks that fall outside the limits, so a tick sitting exactly on a limit is not lost to rounding. Default is 1e-8.

  • label (str or None, optional) – Axis label; omitted when None. Default is None.

  • ticks (sequence of float or None, optional) – Explicit ticks, written without offset or exponent. Default is None, which picks round ticks.

Returns:

The new bar, for more styling by the caller.

Return type:

matplotlib.colorbar.Colorbar

scatterem.vis.visualization_utils.add_colorbars(fig: Figure, ax: Axes, norm: Normalize, cmap: Colormap, *, value_unit: str | None, is_complex: bool, ticks: Any = None) → None#

Add the value colour bar to ax, plus a phase bar for complex data.

The phase bar sits far enough to the right for the tick labels of the value bar. The value bar says “abs” in a title above it, away from its ticks.

Parameters:

  • fig (matplotlib.figure.Figure) – Figure the colour bars belong to.

  • ax (matplotlib.axes.Axes) – Image axes; the bars are appended to its right.

  • norm (matplotlib.colors.Normalize) – Normalization of the shown values. Equal limits (constant data) give one solid colour.

  • cmap (matplotlib.colors.Colormap) – Colour map of the value bar.

  • value_unit (str or None) – Unit of the values: the label of the value bar, or part of its “abs” title for complex data. None shows no unit.

  • is_complex (bool) – Whether the image shows complex data, which adds the phase bar.

  • ticks (sequence of float or None, optional) – Explicit ticks of the value bar, as in add_cbar_to_ax. Default is None, which picks round ticks.

scatterem.vis.visualization_utils.special_ticks(data: Any, role: str) → ndarray | None#

Colour-bar ticks for data that round ticks describe badly.

Constant data gets one tick at its value. Data with the role labels and at most 20 distinct integer values gets one tick per value.

Parameters:

  • data (array_like) – The displayed values (the amplitude, for complex data).

  • role (str) – Colour role of the data.

Returns:

The ticks, or None when round ticks are fine.

Return type:

numpy.ndarray or None

scatterem.vis.visualization_utils.add_scalebar_to_ax(ax: Axes, array_size: float, sampling: float | None, length_units: float | None, units: str | None, width_px: float, pad_px: float, color: str, loc: str | int) → None#

Positional adapter for scatterem.vis.scale_bar.draw_scale_bar().

The drawing lives in scatterem.vis.scale_bar; this signature exists because the figure scripts and ScalebarConfig already speak it.

Two arguments are reinterpreted on the way through, because their names describe the old AnchoredSizeBar implementation rather than the geometry:

width_px

Bar thickness. Was a count of data pixels; now converted to the fraction of the axes height it corresponds to, so it means the same thing on screen for a square image.

pad_px

Corner inset. Was in multiples of the label font size despite the name. Now read as a fraction of the axes – 0.5 was the old default and landed a little inside the corner, so values in that range map to a comparable inset, while a caller who passes a pixel count no longer pushes the bar into the middle of the image.

Prefer draw_scale_bar in new code: it names its arguments after what they do and returns the length it drew.

Parameters:

  • ax (matplotlib.axes.Axes) – Axes to draw the scale bar into.

  • array_size (float) – Width of the displayed array, in pixels.

  • sampling (float or None) – Physical units per pixel; None leaves the bar uncalibrated.

  • length_units (float or None) – Bar length in units; None picks a round length.

  • units (str or None) – Unit label shown next to the bar.

  • width_px (float) – Bar thickness, in data pixels.

  • pad_px (float) – Corner inset, in multiples of the label font size (legacy AnchoredSizeBar convention).

  • color (str) – Matplotlib colour of the bar and of its label.

  • loc (str or int) – Corner that holds the bar, as a matplotlib legend location.

scatterem.vis.visualization_utils.estimate_scalebar_length(n_pixels: float, sampling: float) → tuple[float, float]#

A round bar length for an image n_pixels wide at sampling per pixel.

Thin adapter over scatterem.vis.scale_bar.nice_bar_length(), kept because callers want the length in pixels as well.

Parameters:

  • n_pixels (float) – Width of the displayed array, in pixels.

  • sampling (float) – Physical size of one pixel.

Returns:

(length_in_units, length_in_pixels), or (0.0, 0.0) when the geometry is degenerate – a zero or negative sampling produces no bar rather than a divide-by-zero and a NaN one.

Return type:

tuple
